title: Own wellbeing, resilience and emotional intelligence
blurb: Recognise when you or a colleague is struggling, act to keep patients and staff safe, and build resilience for practice.
question: A colleague confides that she has been drinking heavily since a bereavement and came to work this morning feeling unwell. She asks you to keep it quiet. What should you do?

teach.h: Your health is part of safe practice
teach.body: Code 20.9 requires every registrant to maintain the level of health they need to carry out their professional role. This is not about being perfectly well: it is about noticing when stress, fatigue or illness may affect your practice and acting on it. Plain English: look after yourself so you can look after others, and speak up early when you or a colleague is struggling.

head: Standard
What it asks
rows: Maintain the level of health you need for your role
Support colleagues with health or performance problems, never at the expense of safety
Tell someone in authority early if problems may stop you working within the Code
Take account of your own personal safety as well as patients'

bands.label: Unsafe: impaired at work, risk to patients

teach.caption: Act early. At level 4 patient safety comes first, alongside support for the person.

teach.h: Supporting a colleague without compromising safety
teach.body: Code 8.7 asks you to be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems, but this support must never compromise patient or public safety. If a colleague may be unfit to practise safely right now, you must act on the immediate risk by informing the person in charge, while treating your colleague with compassion and pointing them to support such as occupational health.

root.label: Is there a risk to patients now?

children.label: Inform the nurse in charge now

teach.caption: Either way, encourage them to speak to their manager or occupational health.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Daniel in A&E
teach.body: Daniel's colleague Chloe smells of alcohol at the start of a shift and admits heavy drinking since her father died. She begs him not to tell. Daniel speaks to her kindly, explains he cannot keep it quiet because patients could be harmed, and informs the nurse in charge, who stops her working that shift. Daniel encourages Chloe to contact occupational health and confidential support services.

items: Self-awareness: notice your own emotions and stress signs before they affect care.
Self-regulation: pause before reacting; take breaks; use clinical supervision and debriefs.
Empathy and social skills: recognise how others feel and respond with compassion (Code 2.6).
Reflection: use feedback and reflection to learn rather than to blame yourself (Code 9.2).
Uncertainty: accept that not every situation is clear; escalate and seek help when unsure (Code 13.3).

teach.h: Health conditions and fitness to practise
teach.caption: NMC guidance (2025): being signed off sick, or having a long-term condition or disability, does not necessarily mean fitness to practise is impaired.

teach.text: Supporting a colleague does NOT mean keeping an unsafe situation secret. Code 8.7 says support must never be at the expense of patient or public safety.

items: Code 20.9: maintain the health you need for your role.
Code 8.7: support struggling colleagues, but never at the expense of safety.
Code 16.3: tell someone in authority early if problems may stop you working within the Code.
A health condition does not by itself mean impaired fitness to practise; insight and support matter.

summary: You can now recognise signs that you or a colleague are struggling and respond in a way that is compassionate yet keeps patients safe. You can also describe how resilience, reflection and emotional intelligence support safe practice under pressure.

A.q: Which Code standard requires registrants to maintain the level of health they need to carry out their professional role?
options: Standard 13.4
Standard 20.9
Standard 8.2
Standard 22.3
A.why: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role.

whyNot.0: 13.4 is about taking account of your own personal safety.
whyNot.2: 8.2 is about effective communication with colleagues.
whyNot.3: 22.3 is about keeping knowledge and skills up to date.

A.q: A nurse notices that a usually reliable colleague has become tearful, is making small errors and is arriving late. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Report her to the NMC for poor performance
Correct the errors without mentioning them
Tell other staff to keep an eye on her
Speak privately to her and offer support
A.why: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems. A private, supportive conversation is the first step, while staying alert to patient safety.

whyNot.0: An NMC referral is not a first step for early signs of stress.
whyNot.1: Covering errors silently risks patient safety and offers no support.
whyNot.2: Discussing her with others breaches her dignity and does not help her.

A.q: A nurse has had little sleep for several nights because of a family crisis and feels she may make mistakes. What does Code 16.3 ask her to do?
options: Work extra carefully and keep it to herself
Take unplanned leave without notice
Tell someone in authority early
Swap to night shifts to rest by day
A.why: Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity if you experience problems that may prevent you working within the Code.

whyNot.0: Hiding the problem leaves a risk unmanaged.
whyNot.1: Leaving without notice creates an unsafe staffing gap.
whyNot.3: Changing shifts does not address the risk or involve her manager.

B.q: At the start of a shift, a colleague appears intoxicated and asks you not to tell anyone. What should you do?
options: Inform the nurse in charge straight away
Allocate her lighter patients for the shift
Agree to keep quiet if she goes home
Give her coffee and review in an hour
B.why: Code 8.7: support for colleagues must never compromise patient safety. An immediate risk must be reported to the person in charge (Code 16.1).

whyNot.1: Any patient contact while impaired is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Agreeing to secrecy leaves the risk unreported and may recur.
whyNot.3: Delaying while she remains on duty puts patients at risk.

B.q: A nurse has type 1 diabetes, which she manages well with adjustments agreed by occupational health. Which statement reflects NMC guidance?
options: She should declare it to the NMC each year
She is legally barred from night shifts
A managed condition need not mean impaired fitness
She should transfer to a non-clinical role
B.why: NMC fitness to practise guidance (2025): a registrant may have a long-term condition or disability and practise safely, with or without adjustments.

whyNot.0: There is no annual NMC declaration for a well-managed health condition.
whyNot.1: There is no legal bar on night work for people with diabetes.
whyNot.3: Moving to a non-clinical role is not required when the condition is managed safely.

B.q: After a patient's unexpected death, a newly qualified nurse feels she failed. Which response best supports her resilience?
options: Advise her to put it behind her and move on
Suggest she avoids similar patients for a while
Tell her that feelings like this pass quickly
Offer a debrief and help her reflect on the event
B.why: Debriefing and structured reflection help staff process events, learn and build resilience (Code 9.2, P1.10).

whyNot.0: Dismissing her feelings does not support learning or wellbeing.
whyNot.1: Avoidance does not build confidence or competence.
whyNot.2: Minimising her distress does not offer support.

C.q: A charge nurse realises he is becoming short-tempered with patients during a long period of short staffing and feels exhausted. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue and use annual leave next month
Avoid patients who are demanding
Ask colleagues to cover his difficult patients
Speak to his manager about workload and wellbeing
C.why: Recognising signs of vulnerability in yourself and acting to minimise risk is part of P1.5. Code 16.3 asks him to tell someone in authority early; staffing concerns should also be escalated.

whyNot.0: Waiting a month leaves the risk to patients and to himself unmanaged.
whyNot.2: Shifting work onto colleagues does not address the cause.

C.q: A colleague tells you she has started taking diazepam from the ward stock to cope with anxiety. What should you do?
options: Report it to the nurse in charge or manager
Advise her to see her GP and keep it between you
Check the stock quietly and replace the tablets
Wait to see whether she stops on her own
C.why: Taking controlled stock is a risk to patients and to her. Support must not compromise safety (Code 8.7), and concerns must be raised without delay (Code 16.1).

whyNot.1: Signposting is kind, but keeping it secret leaves a safety risk unreported.
whyNot.2: Replacing stock conceals an incident and is dishonest.
whyNot.3: Waiting allows the risk to continue.

C.q: A nurse faces a situation where the right decision is unclear and senior help is 30 minutes away. Which approach best reflects managing uncertainty safely?
options: Hold off acting until the senior arrives
Act on the most likely option and seek advice
Follow whatever the relative present suggests
Choose the option that is least work
C.why: Accepting uncertainty means acting within competence on the best available information while seeking help (Code 13.3; P6.11).

whyNot.0: Doing nothing can itself cause harm when action is needed.
whyNot.2: Relatives' views matter, but they cannot replace professional judgement.
whyNot.3: Workload is not a basis for clinical decisions.

reteach.title: Oxygen mask first
reteach.question: Why do airlines tell you to fit your own mask before helping others?

blocks.h: You cannot care well when depleted
blocks.body: If you are exhausted, ill or overwhelmed, your judgement suffers and patients are at risk. Looking after your own health (20.9), and telling someone early when you cannot cope (16.3), is a professional duty, not a weakness. The same goes for colleagues: help them get support, but if they are unsafe now, patients come first.

blocks.text: Kindness to a colleague is never secrecy about a risk. Report immediate risks; support the person at the same time.

explain.body: Maintain the health your role needs. Tell someone in authority early if problems may stop you working within the Code.

test.q: A nurse realises a new medicine she takes makes her drowsy at work. What should she do first?
options: Keep working and drink more coffee
Stop the medicine without advice
Tell her manager and seek advice
Avoid medicines rounds this week
test.why: Code 16.3 and 20.9: tell someone in authority promptly about problems that may prevent safe practice, and seek medical advice.

whyNot.0: Caffeine does not remove the risk.
whyNot.1: Stopping a prescribed medicine without advice may harm her.
whyNot.3: Avoiding one task does not address the wider risk.

explain.body: Be supportive of colleagues with health or performance problems, but never at the expense of patient or public safety.

test.q: Code 8.7 says support for a struggling colleague must never compromise what?
options: The colleague's privacy
Patient or public safety
The ward's budget
The team's morale
test.why: Code 8.7: support must never compromise or be at the expense of patient or public safety.

whyNot.0: Privacy matters, but the Code's limit is safety.
whyNot.3: Morale is not the limit set by 8.7.

explain.body: Being unwell or having a disability does not necessarily mean impaired fitness to practise. Insight, treatment and employer support usually manage the risk locally.

test.q: According to NMC guidance, when is NMC action because of a registrant's ill health most likely to be needed?
options: When there is a risk of harm to patients
When the registrant is signed off sick
When a reasonable adjustment is in place
When the registrant has a disability
test.why: The NMC says intervention for ill health is needed where there is a risk of harm to patients or to public confidence; being signed off or having a condition does not of itself mean impairment.

whyNot.1: Being signed off sick does not necessarily mean impaired fitness to practise.
whyNot.3: Disability does not itself mean impaired fitness to practise.

explain.body: Self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social skill help you stay calm, explain decisions and support others under pressure.

test.q: A nurse feels angry when a relative shouts at her, but pauses, breathes and responds calmly. Which aspect of emotional intelligence is she showing?
options: Empathy
Motivation
Social awareness
Self-regulation
test.why: Self-regulation is managing your own emotional reactions so they do not drive your behaviour.

whyNot.0: Empathy is understanding the relative's feelings rather than controlling her own.
whyNot.2: Social awareness is reading others and the situation.
